name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: Which three properties form the CIA triad that serves as the foundational framework for all information security programs?

answers.text: Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability
Compliance, Identity, and Authentication
Confidentiality, Identification, and Authorization
Cryptography, Integrity, and Auditing

explanations.a: The CIA triad — Confidentiality (preventing unauthorized disclosure of information), Integrity (ensuring data accuracy and trustworthiness), and Availability (ensuring authorized users can access resources when needed) — is the foundational framework for all information security programs per EC-Council CEH v13 guidelines and NIST SP 800-12.
explanations.b: Compliance, Identity, and Authentication are important security concepts but are not the CIA triad. Identity and Authentication are access control components; Compliance is a governance concept. The triad specifically refers to Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability.
explanations.c: While Confidentiality is correct, Identification and Authorization are access control mechanisms under the AAA framework (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting), not CIA triad components. Integrity and Availability complete the triad.
explanations.d: Cryptography and Auditing are security mechanisms used to support and enforce the CIA triad properties, but they are not themselves triad components. The triad is Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: A hospital's patient records system becomes completely inaccessible for six hours after a ransomware attack encrypts all files on the server. Which component of the CIA triad is MOST directly violated?

answers.text: Integrity, because the ransomware modified the file contents
Availability, because authorized users cannot access the records
Confidentiality, because the ransomware operator can read the data
Non-repudiation, because the attacker's identity cannot be confirmed

explanations.a: Integrity is violated when data is altered without authorization. While ransomware does encrypt files (a form of modification), the primary and immediate operational impact in this scenario is that authorized clinical staff cannot access the records at all — the access blockage defines the violation.
explanations.b: Availability ensures that information and systems are accessible to authorized users when required. Ransomware that encrypts files and blocks all access is a direct attack on availability — the system may be online but is completely unusable by legitimate users, making this the dominant CIA violation in the described scenario.
explanations.c: Confidentiality would be violated if the attacker could read or exfiltrate unencrypted patient data. Standard ransomware encrypts data and holds it hostage; the scenario describes an access-blocking event, not confirmed data disclosure. Confidentiality may be a secondary concern but is not the primary violation here.
explanations.d: Non-repudiation is not a component of the CIA triad. It is a related but separate security property that ensures an action or communication cannot be denied by the party that performed it.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: An attacker intercepts network traffic between a client and a banking web server, silently alters transaction amounts in transit, then forwards the modified messages to the server. Which CIA triad component is PRIMARILY compromised by this attack?

answers.text: Availability, because the transaction service may be disrupted
Accountability, because audit logs will show false transaction values
Integrity, because data is modified in transit without authorization
Confidentiality, because the attacker can read message content

explanations.a: Availability is not compromised in this scenario — the banking service remains reachable by both client and server. The attacker forwards the traffic (keeping the service available) while silently modifying it, so availability is unaffected.
explanations.b: Accountability and audit integrity are secondary concerns. Accountability is not a CIA triad component — it is part of the AAA framework. The primary violation is against the data itself, not the audit record.
explanations.c: Integrity ensures that data remains accurate, complete, and unaltered during storage or transmission. A man-in-the-middle attack that modifies financial transaction amounts before forwarding is a textbook integrity violation (MITM/T1557 in MITRE ATT&CK). The receiving bank server accepts falsified data it believes is authentic.
explanations.d: Confidentiality is also affected because the attacker reads the messages, but reading without altering constitutes a confidentiality-only attack. The scenario specifically describes unauthorized modification, making integrity the primary concern. Both violations occur, but integrity is primary.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: A disgruntled employee copies sensitive customer PII to a personal USB drive, then deliberately deletes the original database records before resigning. Listed in the order the violations occurred, which CIA triad properties were compromised?

answers.text: Integrity, then Availability
Availability, then Confidentiality
Integrity, then Confidentiality
Confidentiality, then Availability

explanations.a: Integrity involves unauthorized alteration of data. Copying records to a USB drive is a disclosure event, not an alteration. The first act was copying (confidentiality breach), and deletion of records is an availability breach — not an integrity violation.
explanations.b: Availability was not violated first. The data was fully accessible in the database when the employee copied it to the USB drive. The sequence was disclosure first, then destruction.
explanations.c: Confidentiality was violated first (correct), but deleting the original records is not an integrity violation. Integrity refers to unauthorized modification of data content. Deletion removes the data entirely, which is an availability violation — authorized users can no longer access those records.
explanations.d: The attack occurred in two steps: (1) Copying PII to a USB drive = Confidentiality violation — unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal data to an unauthorized medium. (2) Deleting the original database records = Availability violation — authorized users (other employees, systems) can no longer access that data. This insider threat targets both CIA pillars sequentially.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: In the EC-Council CEH five-phase hacking methodology, which phase immediately follows Reconnaissance and involves actively probing target systems for open ports and running services?

answers.text: Scanning
Gaining Access
Maintaining Access
Covering Tracks

explanations.a: The CEH five-phase hacking methodology proceeds as: (1) Reconnaissance → (2) Scanning → (3) Gaining Access → (4) Maintaining Access → (5) Covering Tracks. Scanning is the active phase where attackers probe the target using tools like Nmap or Nessus to identify open ports, running services, OS versions, and potential vulnerabilities — building on passive recon data to identify attack vectors.
explanations.b: Gaining Access is the third phase, not the second. It occurs only after Scanning has identified exploitable vulnerabilities or misconfigurations in the target environment.
explanations.c: Maintaining Access is the fourth phase, focused on establishing persistent backdoors, rootkits, or Trojans after initial access has already been achieved in the prior phase.
explanations.d: Covering Tracks is the fifth and final phase, where the attacker attempts to erase evidence of intrusion by clearing logs, modifying timestamps, and removing malicious artifacts.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: During an authorized penetration test, a tester successfully exploits a buffer overflow vulnerability and then installs a rootkit on the target system to ensure continued access. According to the CEH hacking methodology, which phase is the tester now in?

answers.text: Reconnaissance, gathering information for future attacks
Maintaining Access, establishing persistence on the compromised system
Scanning, identifying additional vulnerabilities on the system
Covering Tracks, erasing evidence of the initial exploitation

explanations.a: Reconnaissance is the very first phase — gathering information about the target before any exploitation occurs. Installing a rootkit requires prior exploitation and represents post-access activity, far beyond the reconnaissance phase.
explanations.b: Maintaining Access is the phase where attackers install backdoors, rootkits, Trojans, or scheduled tasks to ensure they can return to the compromised system even if the initial vulnerability is patched. Installing a rootkit immediately after exploitation is the defining activity of this phase in the CEH methodology.
explanations.c: Scanning is the second phase, performed before gaining access. Running additional scans on an already-compromised system would be part of post-exploitation enumeration but the rootkit installation itself is Maintaining Access.
explanations.d: Covering Tracks involves clearing log files, modifying timestamps, and removing tools to erase evidence of intrusion. While rootkits can assist with hiding files and processes, the act of installing the rootkit for persistence belongs to the Maintaining Access phase.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: Which adversary framework organizes real-world attacker behavior into 14 tactic categories — including Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Exfiltration — and is the industry-standard reference for mapping threats to defensive controls?

answers.text: OWASP Top 10
NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)
MITRE ATT&CK Framework
PTES (Penetration Testing Execution Standard)

explanations.a: The OWASP Top 10 is a ranked list of the most critical web application security risks (e.g., A01 Broken Access Control, A03 Injection). It does not organize adversary behaviors into tactic categories like Initial Access or Exfiltration — it is specific to web application vulnerabilities.
explanations.b: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) organizes security activities into five functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. It is a risk management and governance framework, not a taxonomy of attacker tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
explanations.c: MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) is a globally accessible knowledge base of adversary TTPs derived from real-world observations. Its Enterprise matrix contains 14 tactic categories and hundreds of techniques and sub-techniques, making it the standard reference for threat intelligence, red team planning, and SOC detection engineering.
explanations.d: PTES (Penetration Testing Execution Standard) defines the phases of a penetration test from the tester's perspective (Pre-engagement, Intelligence Gathering, Threat Modeling, Exploitation, Post-exploitation, Reporting). It organizes tester activities, not real-world adversary tactics and techniques.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: A red team uses spear-phishing to deliver a malicious macro (Initial Access), escalates privileges using a local kernel exploit (Privilege Escalation), authenticates to a file server using a captured NTLM hash without the plaintext password, then exfiltrates data via DNS tunneling. When mapping to MITRE ATT&CK, which tactic does using the captured NTLM hash to authenticate to the file server MOST accurately represent?

answers.text: Initial Access — the attacker is gaining a new foothold
Credential Access — the attacker is stealing credentials from the system
Defense Evasion — the attacker is avoiding detection by security tools
Lateral Movement — the attacker is moving to an additional system

explanations.a: Initial Access covers techniques used to gain the first foothold in the network, such as phishing (T1566). The NTLM hash use occurs well after initial access is established and targets a separate system, not the original entry point.
explanations.b: Credential Access (e.g., T1003 OS Credential Dumping) involves stealing credentials or hashes from a compromised system. While a hash must first be obtained (Credential Access) before Pass-the-Hash can be executed, the act of using the hash to authenticate to a remote file server is classified under a different tactic.
explanations.c: Defense Evasion involves techniques to avoid detection, such as obfuscating payloads, disabling security tools, or clearing logs. Using a hash to authenticate does not primarily aim to evade detection — its purpose is to access an additional system.
explanations.d: Pass-the-Hash (MITRE ATT&CK T1550.002 — Use Alternate Authentication Material) is explicitly categorized under the Lateral Movement tactic. It allows an attacker to authenticate to remote systems using captured NTLM hashes without needing the plaintext password, enabling movement from the initially compromised system to additional network resources.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: Which type of hacker operates under explicit written authorization from the target organization to identify and responsibly report security vulnerabilities?

answers.text: White hat hacker
Gray hat hacker
Black hat hacker
Script kiddie

explanations.a: White hat hackers (ethical hackers) are security professionals who are explicitly authorized by the target organization to perform penetration testing and vulnerability assessments. They operate under a formal Rules of Engagement or Statement of Work agreement, report all findings to the client, and work to improve the organization's security posture — the definition of an ethical hacker per EC-Council.
explanations.b: Gray hat hackers operate without explicit permission but typically lack malicious intent. They may discover and disclose vulnerabilities without authorization, sometimes publicly releasing details or requesting payment for remediation information — activities that are still illegal under laws such as the CFAA regardless of intent.
explanations.c: Black hat hackers are malicious actors who compromise systems without authorization for personal gain, espionage, financial fraud, or destructive purposes. They operate entirely outside legal and ethical boundaries.
explanations.d: Script kiddies are unskilled attackers who use pre-written exploit tools and scripts created by others, without understanding the underlying techniques or vulnerabilities. They are distinguished by technical inexperience rather than by authorization status.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: A security researcher independently discovers a critical zero-day in a widely used VPN product, does not notify the vendor, and immediately publishes the full exploit code publicly. Which hacker classification BEST describes this researcher's actions?

answers.text: White hat hacker following responsible disclosure guidelines
Gray hat hacker engaging in full disclosure without vendor notification
Hacktivist pursuing a political agenda against the vendor
State-sponsored actor conducting intelligence operations

explanations.a: Responsible disclosure (coordinated disclosure) requires privately notifying the vendor, providing a remediation window (typically 90 days per Google Project Zero standards), and publishing only after a patch is available. Skipping vendor notification violates this principle, disqualifying the white hat classification.
explanations.b: Gray hat hackers often discover vulnerabilities without authorization and may publish exploit details without a vendor notification period — a practice called full disclosure. They do not typically have malicious financial or destructive intent, distinguishing them from black hats, but their actions are still legally problematic under the CFAA and equivalent international statutes.
explanations.c: Hacktivists are motivated by political, social, or ideological causes and target organizations they oppose. Publishing a technical exploit for a VPN product without an apparent political motive does not fit the hacktivist profile.
explanations.d: State-sponsored actors are government-backed groups conducting intelligence collection, sabotage, or influence operations with significant resources and strategic objectives. An individual researcher publicly releasing exploit code is not indicative of a state-sponsored operation.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: Which term describes a software vulnerability that is actively exploited in the wild but for which the software vendor has not yet released a patch?

answers.text: Legacy vulnerability
Known exploit
Zero-day vulnerability
Residual risk

explanations.a: A legacy vulnerability refers to a flaw in outdated or end-of-life software or systems. It may or may not have an available patch — the distinguishing characteristic is the age and support status of the system, not the absence of a vendor fix.
explanations.b: A known exploit refers to a publicly documented attack technique for a specific vulnerability, typically one for which the vendor has already released a patch. Known exploits are used against unpatched systems — they are the opposite of zero-day situations where no patch exists.
explanations.c: A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw that is unknown to the software vendor or for which no remediation has been released, yet is already being exploited by attackers. The term 'zero-day' refers to the zero days the vendor has had to address the issue. Zero-days command high prices on exploit markets due to their unpatched status.
explanations.d: Residual risk is a risk management concept describing the remaining risk after security controls have been implemented. It is not a term for a specific vulnerability classification.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: A threat group infiltrates a defense contractor, remains undetected for 14 months, systematically exfiltrates classified design blueprints, and uses custom malware that evades all commercial endpoint security products. Which combination of characteristics MOST definitively classifies this as an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)?

answers.text: Use of malware and unauthorized network access
Targeting of a defense sector organization
Use of an encrypted exfiltration channel
Prolonged dwell time, targeted strategic objectives, and custom sophisticated tooling

explanations.a: Use of malware and unauthorized network access are characteristics of virtually all cyberattacks, including low-sophistication opportunistic attacks such as ransomware-as-a-service campaigns. These traits alone do not distinguish an APT from a commodity threat actor.
explanations.b: Defense sector organizations are frequently targeted by APT groups, but sector targeting alone is not a defining characteristic. Ransomware groups and financially motivated actors also target defense contractors for data they can monetize.
explanations.c: Exfiltration over encrypted channels (HTTPS, DNS tunneling) is a standard technique used by both APTs and commodity threat actors. Encryption of exfiltration traffic is not an APT-defining attribute.
explanations.d: APTs are defined by all three attributes simultaneously: Advanced (custom malware evading commercial AV, sophisticated tradecraft), Persistent (14-month dwell time, long-term strategic access rather than hit-and-run), and Threat (specific strategic objective — classified blueprints — rather than opportunistic financial gain). All three pillars together constitute the APT classification per EC-Council CEH v13 and NIST definitions.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: Which pre-engagement document formally defines the IP ranges, systems, permitted attack techniques, timelines, and escalation contacts for a penetration test, and must be signed before any testing begins?

answers.text: Vulnerability Assessment Report
Rules of Engagement (RoE)
Chain of Custody Form
Organizational Security Policy

explanations.a: A Vulnerability Assessment Report is a deliverable produced after testing is complete, documenting discovered vulnerabilities, severity ratings, and remediation recommendations. It is an output, not a pre-engagement authorization document.
explanations.b: The Rules of Engagement (RoE) is a pre-engagement document signed by both the client and the testing team before any activity begins. It defines the scope (target IP ranges, systems, applications), permitted techniques, testing windows, point-of-contact information, and escalation procedures. The RoE provides the ethical hacker with legal authorization and protection under laws such as the CFAA.
explanations.c: A Chain of Custody Form is used in digital forensics investigations to document the handling, transfer, and storage of evidence. It is not an engagement-authorization document for penetration testing.
explanations.d: An Organizational Security Policy defines the company's overall security requirements, acceptable use standards, and governance framework. It is a broad internal governance document, not a specific authorization agreement for a penetration test engagement.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: During a penetration test, a tester discovers a misconfigured server that is explicitly out of scope but appears to contain unencrypted customer Social Security numbers visible in a directory listing. What is the MOST appropriate action?

answers.text: Exploit the server to fully document the extent of the data exposure for the report
Ignore it entirely since it falls outside the defined scope boundaries
Document the observation and immediately notify the designated client contact per the RoE escalation procedure
Access the directory to count the exposed records before deciding whether to report

explanations.a: Exploiting a system that is explicitly out of scope violates the Rules of Engagement and constitutes unauthorized access under the CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030) regardless of the tester's intent. Good intentions do not provide legal protection when operating outside authorized boundaries.
explanations.b: Ignoring a significant security exposure that affects the client's customers fails the core ethical obligation of an ethical hacker. Even out-of-scope observations that pose material risk to the organization or its customers must be communicated to the client.
explanations.c: Ethical hackers have a professional and contractual duty to notify clients of significant security issues discovered during an engagement, even outside the defined scope. The correct action is to document what was observed through incidental discovery (without further accessing the system), stop, and immediately notify the designated client escalation contact per the RoE procedure. The client can then decide how to respond.
explanations.d: Accessing the directory to count records constitutes interaction with an out-of-scope system, which is unauthorized access regardless of the purpose. The tester must not interact with or access out-of-scope systems beyond what was incidentally observed during in-scope activities.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: Which penetration test type provides the tester with zero prior knowledge about the target environment — no network diagrams, no credentials, no system inventory — simulating the perspective of an external attacker?

answers.text: Gray box testing
White box testing
Crystal box testing
Black box testing

explanations.a: Gray box testing provides the tester with partial knowledge of the target environment, such as limited network diagrams, low-privilege credentials, or application user accounts. It simulates an insider with some access, or a partner with limited network knowledge — not a fully external attacker.
explanations.b: White box testing (also called glass box testing) provides the tester with complete knowledge of the target — architecture diagrams, full source code access, administrator credentials, and network maps. It enables the most thorough assessment but least accurately simulates a real external attacker.
explanations.c: Crystal box is an alternate term for white box testing, referring to the complete transparency provided to the tester. It describes the same methodology as white box and is not a distinct separate testing type.
explanations.d: Black box testing simulates a real-world external attacker with no prior knowledge of the target. The tester must rely entirely on reconnaissance and scanning techniques to discover the attack surface, mimicking the perspective of a threat actor who has obtained no insider information about the environment.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: A penetration tester is authorized by a SaaS company to test their customer-facing application. The application runs entirely on AWS infrastructure that the company does not own. In addition to the client's written authorization, what must the tester obtain before testing AWS infrastructure components?

answers.text: Permission from AWS per their Customer Support Penetration Testing Policy
A court order since federal computer access laws require judicial approval
An NDA signed by the AWS security operations team
A prior vulnerability scan report issued by AWS for the target infrastructure

explanations.a: Major cloud providers including AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform maintain Acceptable Use Policies and Penetration Testing Policies that require customers to comply with their terms before conducting security tests against shared infrastructure. AWS's policy (aws.amazon.com/security/penetration-testing) specifies permitted and prohibited activities. Testing without provider awareness may violate cloud service agreements and potentially laws governing unauthorized computer access, even with client authorization.
explanations.b: Court orders are instruments of law enforcement and judicial proceedings — they are not required for commercial penetration testing engagements. Authorization is obtained through a signed agreement with the system owner (client), not through the court system.
explanations.c: An NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement) governs information confidentiality between parties and is not the mechanism cloud providers use to authorize security testing. AWS uses a formal policy and customer notification process, not NDAs signed by AWS security staff.
explanations.d: A prior vulnerability scan report from AWS describes existing known findings and is not an authorization document. The tester needs permission to conduct new testing activities, not access to prior assessment results from the cloud provider.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.keyword: information security controls defense in depth
questions.text: Which security control type is specifically designed to discourage potential attackers before an incident occurs, using measures such as login warning banners and prominently displayed security camera signage?

answers.text: Corrective
Deterrent
Detective
Compensating

explanations.a: Corrective controls are implemented after a security incident to minimize damage and restore systems to a secure operational state. Examples include incident response procedures, patch deployment after exploitation, and system restoration from backups — they act in response to an event, not before one.
explanations.b: Deterrent controls discourage potential attackers from attempting an attack by increasing the perceived risk of detection or legal consequence. Classic examples include login warning banners ('Unauthorized access is prohibited and monitored'), visible security cameras at facility entrances, and security awareness programs that signal an organization actively defends itself.
explanations.c: Detective controls identify and alert on security incidents during or after their occurrence. Examples include intrusion detection systems (IDS), SIEM platforms, security audit log reviews, and file integrity monitoring — they observe and report, not prevent or discourage.
explanations.d: Compensating controls are alternative measures implemented when a primary security control cannot be applied due to technical or operational constraints. For example, enhanced monitoring as a substitute for patching an unsupported legacy system.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.keyword: information security controls defense in depth
questions.text: An organization deploys perimeter firewalls, host-based antivirus on all endpoints, file integrity monitoring on critical servers, data loss prevention (DLP) on email, and encrypts all data at rest. This multi-layered approach BEST exemplifies which security strategy?

answers.text: Zero trust architecture
Security through obscurity
Defense in depth
Risk transference

explanations.a: Zero trust architecture is a security model built on the principle of 'never trust, always verify,' requiring continuous authentication and authorization for every user, device, and network flow regardless of location. While defense in depth and zero trust are complementary strategies, the scenario specifically describes overlapping controls at multiple layers — the hallmark of defense in depth rather than zero trust's continuous verification model.
explanations.b: Security through obscurity relies on keeping system details hidden (e.g., concealing software versions, using non-standard ports) as a primary security mechanism. It is widely considered insufficient as a standalone strategy and is not what is described in this scenario.
explanations.c: Defense in depth is the strategy of implementing multiple overlapping security controls at different architectural layers — network (firewall), host (antivirus), file system (FIM), data transmission (DLP), and data storage (encryption) — so that if one control is bypassed, additional layers continue to protect the asset. The scenario describes exactly this layered, multi-technology approach.
explanations.d: Risk transference shifts financial exposure to a third party, typically through cybersecurity insurance or contractual indemnification. It does not describe the implementation of layered technical security controls.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.keyword: information security controls defense in depth
questions.text: A security team deploys a network intrusion detection system (NIDS) that analyzes traffic and generates alerts when attack signatures are matched but takes no automated action to block the traffic. Which security control category does a NIDS PRIMARILY represent?

answers.text: Preventive — it stops attacks before they reach internal systems
Corrective — it restores systems to a secure state after detection
Deterrent — it discourages attackers who know it is deployed
Detective — it identifies and alerts on security events in progress

explanations.a: Preventive controls stop attacks from occurring or reaching their target. A firewall that blocks malicious packets or MFA that prevents unauthorized logins are preventive. A NIDS that only monitors and alerts does not block traffic — the attack still traverses the network, so it is not preventive.
explanations.b: Corrective controls restore systems to a secure operational state after an incident. An NIDS does not itself take corrective action — it generates an alert that a human analyst or SOAR platform then uses to initiate a corrective response.
explanations.c: Deterrent controls discourage attacks by increasing perceived risk. An NIDS may have an incidental deterrent effect if attackers know it exists, but its designed and primary operational function is identification and alerting, not discouragement.
explanations.d: Detective controls identify security events in progress or immediately after they occur. A NIDS continuously monitors network traffic against a signature database and generates alerts when anomalies or known attack patterns are detected — this is precisely the function of a detective control. A NIPS (Intrusion Prevention System) adds inline blocking to also serve as a preventive control.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.keyword: information security controls defense in depth
questions.text: A critical vulnerability exists in an end-of-life SCADA system controlling physical manufacturing equipment. The vendor no longer provides patches and the system cannot be upgraded without a six-month production shutdown. Which security approach BEST addresses this risk while keeping operations running?

answers.text: Apply compensating controls: segment the SCADA system on an isolated network and implement enhanced monitoring with anomaly detection
Accept the risk formally and document it as a known unpatched vulnerability in the risk register
Transfer the risk by acquiring cybersecurity insurance to cover potential losses
Shut down the SCADA system immediately until the vendor releases a patch

explanations.a: Compensating controls are the recognized approach when primary controls (patching) are technically or operationally infeasible. Network segmentation (creating an isolated OT network zone with strict firewall rules) reduces the attack surface by limiting which systems can communicate with the SCADA controller. Enhanced monitoring with anomaly detection provides detective capability to identify exploitation attempts early. This approach aligns with IEC 62443 industrial security standards and NIST SP 800-82 (Guide to ICS Security), which explicitly recommend these measures for legacy OT environments.
explanations.b: Formal risk acceptance is appropriate for low-impact findings but inadequate for a critical vulnerability in a SCADA system controlling physical equipment. Risk acceptance without additional mitigating controls leaves the organization fully exposed to exploitation that could cause physical damage or safety incidents.
explanations.c: Cybersecurity insurance transfers financial risk but does not reduce the technical probability or operational impact of exploitation. If the SCADA system is compromised, insurance may cover financial losses but cannot prevent physical equipment damage, production disruption, or safety hazards.
explanations.d: Shutting down a SCADA system that controls physical manufacturing equipment would halt production operations — in most industrial environments this causes greater operational and financial harm than managing the vulnerability through compensating controls while planning a controlled upgrade.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: Which U.S. federal statute specifically criminalizes unauthorized access to computer systems and serves as the primary legal basis under which unauthorized hacking is prosecuted in the United States?

answers.text: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act)
CFAA (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act)
SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley Act)
GLBA (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act)

explanations.a: HIPAA establishes privacy and security requirements for protected health information (PHI) held by covered entities and business associates. While HIPAA violations may accompany a cyberattack on healthcare data, HIPAA itself does not criminalize unauthorized computer access.
explanations.b: The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), codified at 18 U.S.C. § 1030, is the primary U.S. federal statute criminalizing unauthorized access to computer systems, unauthorized access to obtain information, computer fraud, and causing damage to protected computers. Ethical hackers obtain written authorization specifically to avoid CFAA criminal and civil liability.
explanations.c: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) establishes internal control and financial reporting requirements for publicly traded companies (enforced by the SEC). While SOX mandates IT controls over financial systems, it does not criminalize unauthorized computer access.
explanations.d: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) requires financial institutions to protect consumer financial information through privacy notices and security programs. Like HIPAA, it imposes data protection obligations but does not specifically prosecute unauthorized hacking.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: A retail company processes Visa and Mastercard transactions across 200 store locations. Which security standard must the company comply with to protect cardholder data, and what entity enforces compliance?

answers.text: HIPAA, enforced by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)
SOX, enforced by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
PCI DSS, enforced through contracts by the payment card brands and acquiring banks
GDPR, enforced by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB)

explanations.a: HIPAA applies to covered entities (healthcare providers, insurers, clearinghouses) and their business associates handling protected health information (PHI). It does not apply to payment card data or retail transaction processing.
explanations.b: SOX applies to publicly traded companies and their financial reporting and internal control requirements. While SOX may impose IT controls on financial systems, it is not the specific standard governing payment cardholder data protection.
explanations.c: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) is the global security standard governing organizations that process, store, or transmit payment card data. It is developed by the PCI Security Standards Council but enforced contractually through the payment card brands (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, Discover) and acquiring banks. Non-compliance can result in fines, higher transaction fees, increased auditing requirements, or termination of the ability to accept card payments.
explanations.d: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies to the processing of personal data of EU/EEA residents. While payment card data qualifies as personal data under GDPR, PCI DSS is the specific standard for cardholder data security. The EDPB enforces GDPR, not PCI DSS.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: Under the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), within what maximum timeframe must a data controller notify the relevant supervisory authority after becoming aware that a personal data breach has occurred?

answers.text: 24 hours
48 hours
30 calendar days
72 hours

explanations.a: A 24-hour notification requirement does not exist under GDPR for supervisory authority notification. Some sector-specific regulations (such as certain financial industry rules in the EU) impose shorter windows, but GDPR Article 33 sets 72 hours as the supervisory authority notification deadline.
explanations.b: A 48-hour window is not mandated by GDPR for supervisory authority breach notification. This timeframe may be confused with internal incident response SLAs or other non-GDPR regulations.
explanations.c: 30 calendar days is far beyond the GDPR supervisory authority notification requirement. This timeframe is associated with some U.S. state data breach notification laws (e.g., certain state statutes for consumer notification), not GDPR's 72-hour supervisory authority requirement.
explanations.d: GDPR Article 33 requires that where a personal data breach is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the data controller must notify the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of the breach. If notification is not possible within 72 hours, the controller must provide reasons for the delay.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.text: A penetration testing firm is engaged to assess the security of a U.S. hospital's EHR system containing electronic Protected Health Information (ePHI). Which combination of legal and compliance requirements is MOST critical before the engagement begins?

answers.text: Obtain written authorization per CFAA requirements and execute a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with the hospital addressing ePHI handling under the HIPAA Security Rule
File a pre-engagement notice with HHS and obtain a HIPAA security testing waiver
Comply with PCI DSS requirements since hospitals also process payment card data
Obtain a federal court order since ePHI is federally protected health data

explanations.a: Two overlapping legal frameworks apply: (1) CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030) requires written authorization from the system owner before any computer access — without it, even authorized-seeming testing is a federal crime. (2) HIPAA Security Rule (45 CFR Part 164) designates the testing firm as a Business Associate that must sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with the covered entity. The RoE must address how incidentally encountered ePHI will be protected, handled, and not retained beyond what is necessary for the assessment.
explanations.b: There is no HIPAA requirement to file a pre-engagement notice with HHS (Department of Health and Human Services) or obtain a testing waiver before conducting a penetration test. HIPAA does not require government pre-approval for security testing activities — it requires appropriate safeguards, contractual protections (BAA), and minimum necessary access.
explanations.c: PCI DSS governs the protection of payment cardholder data and applies where payment cards are processed. A hospital may be subject to PCI DSS for billing systems, but PCI DSS compliance does not address ePHI security requirements or provide authorization to access HIPAA-covered systems.
explanations.d: Federal court orders are used in law enforcement and legal proceedings, not commercial penetration testing. Written authorization from the covered entity (hospital) and a signed BAA constitute the correct legal mechanism — court orders are not part of the penetration testing engagement process.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.keyword: cyber kill chain attack lifecycle stages
questions.text: In the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain model, which stage specifically involves the attacker sending a phishing email with a malicious attachment to a target employee?

answers.text: Weaponization
Exploitation
Delivery
Reconnaissance

explanations.a: Weaponization is the stage preceding delivery where the attacker creates or prepares the malicious payload — for example, embedding an exploit into a Word document macro or PDF. This occurs before the email is sent, not during the act of sending it to the target.
explanations.b: Exploitation occurs after delivery — it is when the malicious payload activates and exploits a vulnerability on the victim's system, such as when the target opens the attachment and the macro executes shellcode.
explanations.c: Delivery is the stage in the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain (2011) where the attacker transmits the weaponized payload to the target environment. Sending a phishing email with a malicious attachment is the canonical example of the Delivery phase — the attacker's objective is to transport the payload to the victim.
explanations.d: Reconnaissance is the first stage where the attacker profiles the target — researching employees, identifying email addresses via LinkedIn, and mapping organizational structure. Reconnaissance precedes all subsequent stages including creating and sending the malicious email.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.keyword: cyber kill chain attack lifecycle stages
questions.text: After a successful phishing attack, malware on the victim's machine sends outbound HTTPS requests to an external IP every 60 seconds to receive attacker commands. Which stage of the Cyber Kill Chain does this beaconing activity represent?

answers.text: Installation — the malware is establishing itself on the system
Weaponization — the attacker is finalizing the payload configuration
Reconnaissance — the malware is profiling the victim's environment
Command and Control (C2) — the compromised system is communicating with attacker infrastructure

explanations.a: Installation is the stage where the malware establishes persistence on the victim system — for example, adding registry run keys, creating a scheduled task, or installing a service. Periodic outbound communications to receive commands represent post-installation attacker control, not the installation event itself.
explanations.b: Weaponization is a pre-attack stage where the attacker creates the malicious payload before it is delivered. The described activity occurs on the victim's machine after the entire attack sequence through Installation, not during payload preparation.
explanations.c: Reconnaissance occurs before the attack begins and involves information gathering about the target organization. Periodic HTTPS connections from a compromised machine to an external server are post-compromise communications, not pre-attack intelligence gathering.
explanations.d: Command and Control (C2) is the Cyber Kill Chain stage where compromised systems communicate with attacker-controlled infrastructure to receive instructions, download additional tools, or exfiltrate data. Periodic HTTPS beaconing — a common C2 mechanism where malware checks in at regular intervals to receive commands — is the defining activity of the C2 stage, enabling the attacker to maintain interactive control over the implant.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.keyword: cyber kill chain attack lifecycle stages
questions.text: Threat intelligence analysts determine that before an attack, the threat actor used Maltego, Shodan, and LinkedIn to map employee names, email addresses, and internet-facing systems belonging to the target organization. Which Cyber Kill Chain stage describes this pre-attack activity?

answers.text: Reconnaissance (target research and footprinting)
Delivery (weaponized payload transmission)
Exploitation (triggering the target vulnerability)
Actions on Objectives

explanations.a: Reconnaissance is the first stage of the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain, where attackers gather intelligence about the target organization using passive OSINT tools (Maltego for relationship mapping, Shodan for internet-facing device discovery, LinkedIn for employee profiling). This information is used to identify attack vectors, craft targeted phishing lures, and plan subsequent stages.
explanations.b: Delivery involves transmitting the weaponized payload to the target — for example, sending a spear-phishing email to addresses gathered during reconnaissance. Delivery comes after reconnaissance and weaponization have already been completed.
explanations.c: Exploitation is when the delivered payload activates a technical vulnerability on the victim's system. Using OSINT tools to gather information does not exploit any technical flaw in the target's systems.
explanations.d: Actions on Objectives is the final Cyber Kill Chain stage where the attacker achieves their ultimate goal — data theft, destruction, or financial fraud. Reconnaissance is the very first stage, separated from the final objective by five intermediate phases.

questions.name: Information Security and Ethical Hacking Overview
questions.keyword: cyber kill chain attack lifecycle stages
questions.text: A defender wants to disrupt an attack at the earliest possible Kill Chain stage. Threat intelligence indicates the adversary is conducting passive DNS lookups, WHOIS queries, and harvesting employee emails from job postings before attacking. Which defensive measure BEST disrupts the attack at this specific stage?

answers.text: Deploy a WAF to block SQL injection attempts against the web application
Minimize publicly available organizational OSINT and monitor for reconnaissance activity via threat intelligence feeds
Enable multi-factor authentication on all remote access and VPN systems
Implement network segmentation to restrict lateral movement after initial compromise

explanations.a: A WAF blocking SQL injection targets the Exploitation stage — when an attacker is actively attacking the web application. The described activity (DNS lookups, WHOIS queries, email harvesting) occurs during Reconnaissance, well before any exploitation attempt.
explanations.b: The described activity occurs during the Reconnaissance stage. Defenses that disrupt this stage include: minimizing publicly available information (removing excess WHOIS data, limiting job posting details, scrubbing employee info from the public web), using privacy guards on domain registrations, and subscribing to threat intelligence feeds that detect when your assets are being profiled by known threat actors. Disrupting reconnaissance forces attackers to work harder or switch targets — the earliest possible Kill Chain intervention.
explanations.c: MFA on remote access systems primarily disrupts the Gaining Access phase by making credential-based attacks harder. It does not address reconnaissance — the attacker can still gather OSINT data regardless of MFA deployment.
explanations.d: Network segmentation restricts lateral movement, which occurs in the Maintaining Access / post-exploitation phase — after the initial compromise has already succeeded. It does not affect the Reconnaissance stage activity described in the scenario.
